title: Why Do So Few Women Work in India?
gist: India's female labor force participation rate is 35%, below Bangladesh (42%) and the Philippines (50%), and the authors argue the binding constraint is weak labor demand rather than social norms — with over 70% of the rise since 2017-18 coming from agriculture and subsistence work marked by disguised employment.

insights.claim: India's female labor force participation rate stands at 35%, well below peer economies Bangladesh at 42% and the Philippines at 50%.
insights.speaker: Shishir Gupta
insights.so_what: A quantified labor-supply gap in the world's most populous economy: closing it toward Bangladesh-level participation is a multi-year growth and consumption swing factor.
insights.quote: India’s female labor force participation rate (LFPR) stands at 35%, which is well below that of peers like Bangladesh (42%) and the Philippines (50%).
insights.locator: NEW DELHI—India's female labor force participation rate

insights.claim: The headline improvement in Indian female participation from 21% in 2017-18 to 35% is largely illusory, because over 70% of the increase came from agriculture and subsistence sectors with significant disguised employment.
insights.speaker: Shishir Gupta
insights.so_what: Treat India's reported employment gains as low-quality: they imply weaker formal wage income and consumer-spending power than the headline LFPR series suggests.
insights.quote: over 70% of the increase came from the agriculture and subsistence sectors, with significant levels of disguised employment
insights.locator: Though it has risen substantially from 21% in 2017–18

insights.claim: Low female participation in India is a demand-side labor problem rather than a product of social norms, meaning the constraint sits with employers and regulation, not culture.
insights.speaker: Shishir Gupta
insights.so_what: Reframes the India female-employment debate: the investable lever is job creation and regulatory reform, not slow-moving cultural change.
insights.quote: not because of social norms, but because of weak demand for labor
insights.locator: India’s female labor force participation rate has long lagged

insights.claim: Because the constraint is demand for labor, it is tractable through common-sense regulatory reform and public investment, making the shortfall a solvable policy problem rather than a structural ceiling.
insights.speaker: Shishir Gupta
insights.so_what: Frames Indian labor-reform and capex announcements as the catalysts to watch for an inflection in female employment and household income.
insights.quote: it is a problem that can be solved with common-sense regulatory reforms and public investment
